title: What is expected return?
subtitle: Expected Return is a probability-weighted average across every possible scenario.
openingQuestion: You invest 100 million. There's a 60% chance of a 20% gain, a 40% chance of a 10% loss. What is the expected return?
openingOptions: It can't be calculated, since the outcome isn't known yet
20%, because the chance of winning is higher
explanation: Expected return is a probability-weighted average across every scenario: multiply each probability by its outcome, then add them up. The part that trips people up is that this is a long-run number, not a forecast of what happens next time. An investment with a 60% chance of a 20% gain and a 40% chance of a 10% loss has an expected return of 8%, but any single outcome can only be +20% or −10% - never exactly 8%.

Multiply each probability by its outcome, then add
The result is a long-run average, not a single outcome

realWorldExample.description: The S&P 500 has a long-run expected return of roughly 10% a year. But in any single year, it has swung from -37% to +38%. The expected value is the average across countless scenarios.

quiz.question: Why doesn't expected return guarantee the actual outcome?
options: Because it's a long-run average, not a figure for any single year
Because the initial probability estimates are almost always wrong
Because the formula always contains some fixed rounding error
Because inefficient markets mean prices misprice risk
quiz.explanation: An expectation of 8% means an average across many repetitions. On any single occasion, you might get 20% or lose 10%. The spread around the expected value is exactly what risk is.

quiz.question: What does the Sharpe Ratio measure?
options: The total return a portfolio achieved during the year
The excess return divided by the standard deviation
The standard deviation divided by the excess return
The probability a portfolio loses money in any given year
quiz.explanation: Sharpe Ratio = (portfolio return − the risk-free rate) / standard deviation. It measures the return earned per unit of risk taken on. A higher Sharpe means greater efficiency.

quiz.question: Scenario: You're choosing between two funds. Fund A: expected return 15% a year, standard deviation 20%. Fund B: expected return 12% a year, standard deviation 10%. The risk-free rate is 6%. Which fund has the better Sharpe Ratio, and what is it?
options: Fund A is better, Sharpe = 0.75 (forgetting to subtract 6%)
Fund A is better, Sharpe = 0.45
Fund B is better, Sharpe = 0.60
Fund B is better, Sharpe = 0.90 (forgetting to subtract 6%)
quiz.explanation: Sharpe A = (15% − 6%) / 20% = 0.45. Sharpe B = (12% − 6%) / 10% = 0.60. Fund B's higher Sharpe means it generates more excess return per unit of risk accepted.

quiz.question: Scenario: An investment has a 50% chance of a 20% gain, a 30% chance of a 5% gain, and a 20% chance of a 10% loss. What is the expected return?
options: 5% (= taking the middle scenario as representative)
15% (= (20 + 5 + 10) ÷ 3, ignoring the probabilities)
quiz.explanation: The expectation is the sum of probability times outcome: 10 + 1.5 − 2 = 9.5%. Taking a simple average of the scenarios is the most common mistake - it implicitly assumes every scenario is equally likely, which is almost never true.

quiz.question: Scenario: Fund A expects 15% a year with a standard deviation of 20%. Fund B expects 10% with a standard deviation of 8%. The risk-free rate is 4%. Which fund has the higher Sharpe Ratio?
options: B, because (10−4)/8 = 0.75 is higher than 0.55
A, because its expected return of 15% is higher than 10%
A, because (15−4)/20 = 0.55 is the higher figure
They're equal, because both compensate for risk the same way
quiz.explanation: Sharpe measures the return above the risk-free rate per unit of volatility taken on: A gives 0.55, B gives 0.75. B earns less in absolute terms, but gets more back for every percentage point of risk taken - and if you leveraged B up to match A's level of risk, B would still come out ahead.

keyTakeaways: Expected Return = the sum of (probability × outcome) across every scenario
The expectation is a long-run average; it doesn't guarantee any short-run outcome
Sharpe Ratio: excess return earned per unit of risk

practicePrompt.question: You have two options for investing 100 million VND for 1 year. Option A: 70% chance of a 10% gain, 30% chance of a 5% loss. Option B: 50% chance of a 20% gain, 50% chance of an 8% loss. Which option has the higher expected return?
options: Option B, because its expected return is 6% (0.5×20% + 0.5×(-8%)), higher than option A
Option A, because its expected return is 7% (0.7×10%), higher than option B
The two are equal, because each pair of probabilities adds up to 100%
They can't be compared, because expected return only means something once the outcome is known for certain
practicePrompt.explanation: Option A: 0.7×10% + 0.3×(-5%) = 5.5%. Option B: 0.5×20% + 0.5×(-8%) = 6%. Even though B has a higher chance of a loss, its expected value is still higher than A's.

summary.keyIdea: Expected Return = the sum of (probability × outcome) across every scenario
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: The expectation is a long-run average; it doesn't guarantee any short-run outcome

application.title: Calculate the expected return for a real decision
application.message: Pick a financial decision you're weighing, estimate 2-3 possible scenarios with a probability for each, then calculate expected return = the sum of (probability × outcome) as in this lesson.
application.secondary: Don't worry about the number being exactly right - the habit of doing this matters more than the answer itself.

sections.text: You invest 100 million. A 60% chance of a 20% gain, a 40% chance of a 10% loss. What is the expected return? This is one of the most important calculations for making an investment decision on solid ground.

Expected Return is a weighted average of every possible outcome, with the weight being each outcome's probability. **Formula:** Expected Return = Σ (probability × outcome). In the example above: 0.6 × 20% + 0.4 × (−10%) = 12% − 4% = 8%.
An expectation isn't a certain prediction

The point most easily misunderstood: the 8% figure doesn't mean 'the actual outcome will be 8%'. On any single occasion, the actual outcome can only be +20% or −10% (never exactly 8%). The 8% only means something if this situation repeats many, many times - it is a long-run average, not a promise for any single instance.

items: Expected Return = the sum of (probability × outcome) across every possible scenario
The expectation is a long-run average across many repetitions, not a guarantee for any single occasion
Sharpe Ratio: measures excess return (over the risk-free rate) per unit of risk accepted

sections.label: Applying it to a portfolio
sections.text: Expected Return is the foundation for comparing different investment opportunities quantitatively, instead of relying on a gut feeling that something 'sounds good'. It's also the first step toward building a properly diversified portfolio.

lines: A skilled investor doesn't only ask 'how much could I win', but always accounts for both the probability and the size of the losing scenario to get the full picture.
